# The Weight of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how rarely we acknowledge the strangeness of being alive. We move through our days collecting small experiences like lint in a pocket—a stranger's laugh at the coffee shop, the way light breaks through clouds, the peculiar comfort of an old sweater—and we rarely stop to consider how miraculous it is that we're here at all, aware, noticing things.

There's something I noticed this morning while waiting for the kettle to boil. I was watching the steam rise, those ghost-like wisps disappearing into the kitchen air, and I thought about how I've probably watched this same phenomenon ten thousand times in my life, maybe more, and yet this was the first time I actually *saw* it. Really saw it. The first time I considered that those molecules of water were transforming from liquid to vapor, that they were changing their very nature before my eyes, and that I was privileged enough to witness this ordinary miracle while standing in my kitchen in comfortable clothes on a Tuesday morning.

That's when it hit me: most of life is like this. Most of what makes existence profound isn't the big moments—the graduations, the weddings, the disasters. It's the unremarkable Tuesday mornings. It's the fact that we somehow have consciousness at all, that we can think about our thinking, that we can recognize patterns and create meaning from them.

I wonder if this awareness is a gift or a curse. Sometimes I think my brain is too loud, always analyzing, always noting, always trying to extract significance from insignificance. My friends would tell me I overthink things. They're probably right. There's a part of me that envies people who can simply exist without constantly narrating their existence to themselves. People who just *are* without spending so much energy thinking about *being*.

But then again, isn't that narration the most essentially human thing we do? We're storytelling creatures. We can't help but make sense of the world through narrative. Even when I'm not consciously writing or speaking, my brain is writing a continuous story: "Here I am, doing this, noticing that, feeling this way about it." It's exhausting sometimes, but it's also the only way I know how to be.

I've been reading a lot lately about consciousness and neuroscience, trying to understand what makes the experience of being me different from the experience of being, say, a dog or a tree. And the honest answer that keeps emerging from the research is: we don't really know. We can map the brain, track the firing of neurons, measure electrical impulses, and yet the actual subjective experience—what philosophers call qualia—remains fundamentally mysterious. Why does red look the way it looks? Why does sadness feel different from loneliness? Why does time seem to move slower when you're bored and faster when you're engaged?

There are no good answers to these questions. And maybe that's the point. Maybe the mystery is essential to the experience.

I've also been thinking about time, which I suspect everyone does more as they get older. When I was young, a year felt impossibly long. Summers stretched out like infinity. Now a year feels like a paragraph in a book I'm reading too quickly. I blink and another season has changed. I suspect this happens because each year becomes a smaller percentage of your total lived experience. When you're ten, a year is ten percent of your life. When you're forty, it's two and a half percent. The math is simple, but the implications are vertiginous.

This is why people say to be present. This is why mindfulness is suddenly everywhere—in apps and podcasts and books and wellness centers. We're all dimly aware that time is a slippery thing, that it accelerates without our permission, and that if we don't pay attention, we'll blink and miss our lives entirely.

The problem is that presence is hard. It's cognitively exhausting to actually pay attention to your life as it's happening. It's much easier to slip into autopilot, to live through your experiences rather than in them. Most of my commute is like this—I arrive at my destination with no memory of how I got there. Most of my meals are consumed while my mind is elsewhere. Most of my conversations are interrupted by the urge to check my phone.

We live in an age of unprecedented distraction. We carry around devices designed specifically to fragment our attention. They're not evil exactly; they're just optimized for engagement, and our brains evolved in an environment where immediate attention to stimuli was often a matter of survival. We're not built to resist the ping of a notification. We're not wired to ignore a flashing light. We're ancient brains in a modern world, and the modern world is winning.

And yet, despite all this, moments of genuine presence still happen. They're rarer than they used to be, but they still arrive unbidden. A conversation with a friend that becomes so absorbing that you lose track of time. A book that pulls you so completely into its world that you forget about your own problems. A song that plays and suddenly you're dancing in your kitchen and laughing at yourself for dancing in your kitchen.

These moments are like oxygen. After enough time in the low-oxygen environment of distraction and autopilot, these moments of real presence feel vital.

I don't have any conclusions about any of this. I'm not offering wisdom or a solution or even a particularly coherent argument. I'm just thinking out loud, the way I sometimes do when I have a lot of words in my head and nowhere to put them. I'm noticing things and trying to articulate why I'm noticing them and what it means that I'm noticing them.

Tomorrow the kettle will boil again. The steam will rise. Most of the time I won't pay attention to it. But maybe once or twice a week, I'll remember this morning and pause for a moment and really see it. And maybe that's enough. Maybe noticing something wonderful occasionally is better than never noticing it at all.

Maybe that's enough for all of us.
